title: Roles and responsibilities within projects
apm_learning_objective: Understand the roles and responsibilities within projects.
exam_coverage_note: 1 of 60 marks. One learning outcome, but it names seven roles and any of them can be the question.
source_ref: APM PFQ Qualification Handbook, APM-QS-PFQ-8 V5 (April 2026), §11d. Syllabus maps this objective to APM Body of Knowledge 7th ed. 1.3.5, 1.3.8, 1.3.10, 2.2.1, 3.3.1 and 8th ed. 2.6.2, 2.6.3, 2.6.4, 3.5.4, 4.1.4, 1.1.3.
competence_area_note: The handbook publishes no per-objective Competence Framework mapping. Left null rather than guessed.
where_this_fits: One outcome and one mark, the smallest objective in the syllabus. The seven roles keep turning up later in the course, so learn them once, quickly, and move on.

key_definitions.definition: The individual accountable for the project's business case and for the realisation of its benefits.
key_definitions.plain_english: The person who wanted this done and who answers for whether it was worth doing.

key_definitions.definition: The individual accountable for the day-to-day management of the project and for delivering its objectives within agreed constraints.
key_definitions.plain_english: The person who runs it and answers for whether it got delivered.

key_definitions.definition: The framework of authority, accountability and decision-making within which a project is directed and controlled.
key_definitions.plain_english: The rules about who can decide what, and what happens when the project goes outside its limits.

key_definitions.definition: The body that exercises project governance, authorising the project to proceed at decision gates and deciding matters beyond the project manager's delegated authority.
key_definitions.plain_english: The group the project manager goes to when a decision is above their pay grade.

key_definitions.definition: An individual accountable to the project manager for delivering allocated work packages.
key_definitions.plain_english: The people doing the work that produces the output.

key_definitions.definition: An individual or group who will use the project's outputs once they are handed over.
key_definitions.plain_english: Whoever ends up having to live with what the project built.

key_definitions.definition: A role in iterative working, accountable for prioritising requirements and deciding what the team delivers next on behalf of those who will use the product.
key_definitions.plain_english: The person who decides what gets built in the next iteration, and in what order.

key_definitions.definition: A function providing standards, processes, tools, reporting and support to projects across an organisation.
key_definitions.plain_english: The team that sets how projects are run here and helps them run that way.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline project management roles and responsibilities
core_content.key_takeaway: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for the project delivering its benefits. The project manager is accountable for day to day management and for delivering the objectives within the constraints. The other named roles are the governance board, which authorises the project at each decision gate, project team members, who do the work, end users, who receive and use the output, the product owner, who prioritises requirements in iterative work, and the project management office, which provides standards, tools and support across projects. Project governance is the framework of authority, accountability and decision making that the project runs inside, and the governance board is the body that exercises it.
core_content.body_markdown:
Learn each role by the duty only it holds, rather than by a list of tasks.

The project sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for the project delivering its benefits. They secure the funding, chair the decision gates, and are the project manager's route to a decision above their own authority. If a question mentions owning, approving, justifying or funding, it is the sponsor.

The project manager is accountable for day to day management and for delivering the objectives within the constraints. They produce the project management plan. If a question mentions planning, coordinating, monitoring or reporting, it is the project manager.

Project governance is the framework of authority, accountability and decision making that the project runs inside. It sets the tolerances the project manager works within. Governance is a framework, not a person.

The governance board is the body that exercises that framework. It authorises the project to continue at each decision gate and rules on changes that go beyond the project manager's delegated limit.

Project team members do the work that produces the outputs, and answer to the project manager for the work packages given to them.

End users are the people who will use the output once it is handed over. Their acceptance decides whether handover succeeds, and their use of it decides whether any benefit appears.

The product owner is an iterative role. They prioritise requirements and decide what the team builds next, on behalf of the people who will use the product.

The project management office provides standards, processes, tools, reporting and support across projects. It supports and enables. It does not own the business case and it does not run individual projects.

The distinction that decides most questions is sponsor against project manager. One owns why the project exists. The other owns how it gets done.

misconceptions.wrong: The project manager owns the business case.
misconceptions.right: The sponsor owns it. The project manager supplies the information that keeps it accurate, which is outcome 4.5.

misconceptions.wrong: The sponsor is the project manager's line manager.
misconceptions.right: The sponsor is accountable for the business case and the benefits. The relationship is about project accountability, not line management, and in many organisations they sit in different reporting lines entirely.
The PMO provides standards, processes, tools and support across projects. Running an individual project is the project manager's job.

misconceptions.wrong: Project governance and the governance board are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: Governance is the framework of authority and accountability. The board is the body that exercises it. One is a set of rules, the other is a group of people.

misconceptions.wrong: End users only matter at handover.
misconceptions.right: Their acceptance decides whether transition succeeds and their adoption decides whether benefits are realised, which is why the extended life cycle runs past handover.

misconceptions.wrong: The product owner is just an iterative name for the project manager.
misconceptions.right: They are separate roles with different accountabilities. The product owner decides what gets built next. The project manager is accountable for delivering it within constraints.

memory_aids.expansion: Sponsor owns why the project exists. Project manager owns how it gets done. The single most examined distinction in this objective.
Any of those three verbs in a question stem points at the sponsor or the governance board, never the project manager.
The PMO's whole position in one phrase. If an option gives the PMO authority over a project decision, it is wrong.
Governance is the framework. The governance board is the body that applies it.

progress_checkpoint: I can name all seven roles in this outcome without looking.
I can give each role its one distinguishing duty in a single sentence.
I can say who owns the business case and who produces the project management plan.
I can explain the difference between project governance and a governance board.
I can say what a PMO does and, more importantly, what it does not do.
I can say what a product owner decides and why that role belongs to iterative working.
